meta_description: Tube amplifier repair in Indianapolis. Bias, retube, full recap, hum and intermittent fault diagnosis on Fender, Marshall, Ampeg, Vox, Mesa, and vintage amps. $45 bench fee, 30-day labor warranty.
intro: Tube amps fail in ways that are easy to guess at and expensive to guess wrong about. A hum can be filter capacitors, a heater fault, a bad ground, or a tube that is only bad under load. Swapping parts until it goes away is how a cheap repair turns into a bill for parts you did not need.

I diagnose first. The amp goes on the bench, I trace the actual fault, and you get findings and a written estimate before any repair work happens. Every job gets documented - what came in, what it turned out to be, and what fixed it.

faults.name: Hum and buzz
faults.detail: Filter capacitors dry out and stop doing their job, and the amp starts amplifying its own power supply ripple. On a recent Deluxe Reverb this showed up first as a blubbery low end under load, then as loud hum at idle.

faults.name: Dead or weak output
faults.detail: Screen resistors, output tubes, and the high-voltage supply are the usual suspects. These are diagnosed against actual voltage readings, not by swapping tubes and hoping.

faults.name: Crackle and intermittents
faults.detail: The hardest category, because the fault has to be present to be found. Dirty pots and jacks, cold solder joints, failing plate resistors, and tube sockets that have lost tension.

faults.name: Bias drift and retubes
faults.detail: New tubes need the bias set for them. An amp running hot eats tubes and output transformers; running cold sounds thin and crossover-distorted.

faults.name: Dead reverb or tremolo
faults.detail: Usually the recovery tube, the tank, or the RCA cables to it - all cheap, all commonly misdiagnosed as something worse.

faults.name: Full recap and restoration
faults.detail: Electrolytics have a service life. On a vintage or hard-used amp, a full recap resets the clock and is often the difference between a reliable amp and one you cannot trust at a gig.

safety_note: Tube amps hold lethal voltage in the filter capacitors after they are unplugged. If you are not set up to discharge and measure them safely, this is not a good first repair to learn on.

faq.q: What brands do you work on?
faq.a: All of them. Fender, Marshall, Vox, Mesa/Boogie, Orange, Peavey, Ampeg, and boutique or vintage amps of any make and era.

faq.q: Do you work on solid-state amps too?
faq.a: Yes. Tube amps are the specialty, but solid-state gets the same diagnostic approach and the same documentation.
A $45 bench fee starts every job and is applied to your total if you approve the work. Labor runs $55-65/hr depending on the job, plus parts at cost + 25%. You get the estimate before I start.

faq.q: Can I ship an amp to you?
faq.a: Yes. Email me first so I can tell you how to pack it. Pull the tubes and the reverb tank and pack them separately - those are what break in transit.

meta_description: Vintage and modern synthesizer repair in Indianapolis. Juno-106 voice chips, BBD chorus, oscillator calibration, key contacts, power supplies, and component-level troubleshooting. Mail-in accepted.
intro: Vintage synths fail at the component level, and the parts that fail are often the ones nobody stocks any more. That is the part most shops will not take on - it means sourcing, testing, and calibrating rather than ordering a board and dropping it in.

I work against service manuals and, where it helps, against a known-good machine on the same bench. Comparing a suspect reading to a healthy one under identical conditions is frequently the only way a drifted part gives itself away.

faults.name: Dead or detuned voices
faults.detail: On a Juno-106 that usually means the 80017A voice chips, which fail predictably with age. A full set replacement plus factory calibration brings the whole machine back into spec.

faults.name: Noisy chorus
faults.detail: The bucket-brigade delay chips get noisier as they age. Verified against the surrounding circuit first - power rails, bias, LFO on the scope - so parts are not swapped on a guess.

faults.name: Drifted calibration
faults.detail: Filter tracking, VCA offset, oscillator tuning, and noise level all drift. Full factory calibration in the sequence the service notes specify, not a quick trim.

faults.name: Oscillator tuning
faults.detail: Analog oscillators that will not stay in tune or track across the keyboard - scaling, high-end trim, and temperature stability.

faults.name: Key contacts and sliders
faults.detail: Unresponsive or double-triggering keys, scratchy sliders, and dead panel controls.

faults.name: Power supplies
faults.detail: Rails out of spec cause faults everywhere downstream and get mistaken for a dozen other problems. Always checked before anything else.

faults.name: Digital workstations
faults.detail: Factory resets, OS and sound data reloads, and boot failures on machines like the Triton where the original media is long gone.

safety_note: If your synth has a backup battery and stored patches you care about, back them up before the battery is replaced - swapping it wipes the memory.

faq.q: Do you work on vintage and modern synths?
faq.a: Both. Moog, Roland, Korg, Sequential, Yamaha, Oberheim, and modern gear too. Vintage work is where the component-level sourcing matters most.
Often, yes. That is a normal part of vintage synth work - finding a correct or genuinely equivalent part, testing it, and calibrating around it.

faq.q: Will a repair change how it sounds?
faq.a: The goal is factory specification, not a reinterpretation. Where a repair genuinely improves on the original - a quieter chorus, for instance - I tell you what changed and why.

faq.q: Can I ship a synth to you?
faq.a: Yes, and small items like voice boards, modules, and chip sets ship cheaply from anywhere. Email me before sending anything.

h1: Hammond, Leslie & Rhodes Service in Indianapolis
meta_title: Hammond Organ, Leslie & Rhodes Repair Indianapolis | Filament
meta_description: Hammond organ, Leslie speaker, and Fender Rhodes service in Indianapolis. AO-28 recapping, 120 Hz hum, Leslie motor service, Rhodes tuning, voicing, and pickup setup.
intro: Electromechanical keyboards are half electronics and half machine, and they need someone willing to work on both. A Leslie that has lost its speed is a mechanical problem. A Hammond that hums is an electronic one. A Rhodes that plays unevenly is neither - it is geometry.
These instruments are old enough that maintenance has usually been deferred for decades. Most of what they need is not exotic, it is just overdue.

faults.name: Hammond hum
faults.detail: A 120 Hz hum through the AO-28 is the classic sign that the power supply filter capacitors are finished. Recapping it is routine, well-documented work.

faults.name: Leslie speed and noise
faults.detail: Dry bearings and glazed drive wheels are why a Leslie will not come up to speed or will not hold one. Motor service, lubrication, and drive surface work.

faults.name: Rhodes tuning and voicing
faults.detail: Tine height, escapement, and pickup position determine both tuning and bark. Setting them across the whole instrument is what makes a Rhodes play evenly.

faults.name: Rhodes electronics
faults.detail: Suitcase preamps and power amps, including hard-to-source parts in the Peterson power amp that are usually written off as unobtainable.

faults.name: Dead keys and contacts
faults.detail: Contact cleaning and adjustment on organs and electric pianos where keys are silent, weak, or inconsistent.

safety_note: These instruments are heavy and awkward, and a Leslie in particular does not travel well. If you are local, drop-off is usually the better call.

faq.a: Yes - motor service, bearings, drive wheels, lubrication, and the electronics.

faq.q: Can you tune and voice a Rhodes?
faq.a: Yes. Full tuning, tine and escapement setup, and pickup positioning across the instrument, not just the notes that are obviously off.

faq.q: Do you do pickup and repair?
faq.a: For heavy instruments locally, that can usually be arranged. Ask when you get in touch.

faq.q: Is a full recap worth it on a Hammond?
faq.a: On an untouched AO-28, generally yes. The capacitors are decades past their service life and the hum they cause will only get worse.

h1: Pro Audio & Outboard Repair in Indianapolis
meta_title: Pro Audio & Outboard Gear Repair Indianapolis | Filament
meta_description: Professional audio and outboard equipment repair in Indianapolis. Preamps, DIs, power supply and rail failures, transformer faults, and backline service by a working backline tech.
intro: I work as a backline technician as well as a bench tech, so professional audio gear is familiar territory rather than an exception. Preamps, DIs, outboard, and touring backline all come through here.
Studio and stage gear tends to fail under conditions that are hard to reproduce on a bench, so diagnosis matters more than usual. I would rather find the fault than replace the board it lives on.

faults.name: Dead or intermittent channels
faults.detail: Traced through the signal path stage by stage rather than swapping modules until it works.

faults.name: Power supply and rail failures
faults.detail: A missing or sagging supply rail takes out everything downstream. On a recent Avalon U5 the positive rail was gone entirely - the cause turned out to be an open transformer winding, not the supply board everyone suspects first.

faults.name: Transformer faults
faults.detail: Open windings and failed input or output transformers, which are frequently misread as a fault in the circuit they feed.

faults.name: Noise and hum
faults.detail: Grounding problems, failing electrolytics, and supply ripple appearing where it should not.

faults.name: Connectors and mechanical
faults.detail: Jacks, switches, and connectors - the parts that actually take the abuse on touring gear.

safety_note: If a piece failed at a show and you need it back fast, say so up front - rush service is available and it changes how I schedule the bench.

faq.q: Do you take touring and backline work?
faq.a: Yes. I work as a backline tech, so this is routine rather than unusual.

faq.q: How fast can you turn something around?
faq.a: Standard is 3-7 business days. Rush service with a 48-hour turnaround is available for an additional $35.

faq.q: Do you work on digital gear?
faq.a: Where the fault is serviceable, yes. If a repair depends on a part or firmware nobody can get any more, I will tell you that instead of billing you to find out.

faq.q: Can I ship outboard gear in?
faq.a: Yes - rack gear and small outboard ship well and I take mail-in work from anywhere. Email me before sending.
